keyVerseText: Then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem. So it ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word אֱלָהּ (ʼĕlâhh, H426) is etymologically linked to the Aramaic אֱלוֹהַּ (ʼĕlôwahh), both referring to a deity or God. Its root sense encompasses both the concept of God as the supreme deity and the broader category of gods, including false gods. This root connection highlights a foundational understanding of divine power and authority, distinguishing the true God of Israel from other deities, which adds depth beyond the simple English term "God."
usageInScripture: This term appears 95 times in the Hebrew Bible, predominantly translated as "of God" (21 times), "God" (15 times), and variations such as "of the God" and "of thy God." Its usage spans references to the God of Israel as well as heathen deities, demonstrating a lexical range that includes both the true God and false gods. This variety in translation reflects the word's flexible application in scripture, underscoring the importance of context when discerning its precise meaning.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding אֱלָהּ in its original linguistic and cultural context is vital for grasping the biblical portrayal of God’s uniqueness and sovereignty. The term’s dual capacity to denote both the true God and false gods reminds believers of the biblical call to worship the one true God alone. It affirms the reality of spiritual opposition while emphasizing God's supreme authority over all. For the Christian faith, this word roots the doctrine of God in the ancient Hebrew understanding, inviting reverence for the God who reveals Himself uniquely in Scripture and ultimately in Christ.
keyVerseReflection: Ezra 4:24 states, "Then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem." Here, the term אֱלָהּ underscores the sacred identity of the temple as God’s dwelling place. The cessation of the work on God's house signifies a divine pause in the restoration of worship and covenantal presence. Recognizing the word אֱלָהּ in this verse enriches our appreciation of the holiness and centrality of God’s house in Israel’s history and faith.
